toc.title: Mixed states, or mixed states in context?

blocks.p: Fawn, appeasement, and intimacy were added to the Polyvagal Theory's mixed states. But is intimacy actually a mixed state, or is it something else? I want to challenge the way you think about the polyvagal mixed states.

With fawn and appeasement, I raised the question of behavioral adaptations versus mixed states. With intimacy, I have a new question: does the context of a mixed state matter? And is that a more helpful framework for the Polyvagal Theory than the mixed state on its own?
The new book, Our Polyvagal World, doesn't have a ton to say about these new mixed states. Intimacy has a couple of pages dedicated to it, I believe. Overall I do recommend the book.

Intimacy is listed as a mixed state, and you can probably guess which states underlie it. Intimacy is being immobile, or largely immobile, but without fear. And it involves being with someone. So there's trust and vulnerability, physical touch, co-regulation. What does that sound like? Shutdown and safety combined together.
Now, the astute polyvagal nerd will say, "Hold on a second. Hold your horses, Justin. The mixed state of shutdown and safety is already taken. That's stillness."
And I would say: yes, you are right, astute polyvagal nerd. Intimacy is basically stillness, but with somebody, with a safe other.
Deb Dana put the vulnerability of stillness well when she was on the podcast:

q: Stillness is the most complicated autonomic blend of states, because how do you come into quiet, into stillness, without stimulating shut down? It's a tricky thing to do, especially for people with a trauma history. Because stillness is a very vulnerable place and I have to really feel safe to come into stillness.
blocks.cite: Deb Dana, [Deb Dana Interview: Story Follows State, Climbing the Ladder and Diagnosing (episode 29)](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/f8b9643c-28f8-4185-9525-8b4e6301516c)

blocks.p: So we already know what that mixed state is. It's stillness. What's different here is that intimacy involves co-regulation, being with a safe other. I think Dr. Porges has referred to co-regulation as an interpersonal neurobiological interaction. I think that's what he called it.

And that raises a more interesting question: what happens when a state or a mixed state involves being with someone? You can be in your safety state with somebody, or you can be in it alone. It can be co-regulative or self-regulative.
Let's look at it in more detail with a few examples.

Safety plus mobility. You already know this one: it's play. But that's safety plus mobility with somebody. What does safety plus mobility equal when you're alone? I'd say it's exercise. That's not play anymore, because there's no co-regulation. You're by yourself, but you're mobile, in safety.

So would we call exercise a new mixed state? Kind of could. It makes sense. Or would we say there's an element of play when you're alone? I don't think so, because Dr. Porges is very explicit that play is an interpersonal neurobiological interaction. So I don't think we'd say exercise is a form of play. It might just be the mixed state of safety plus mobility in a different context. Or maybe it's safety plus mobility, plus whether or not someone is there.

Safety plus shutdown. That's the one we already went over. Alone, it's stillness. With somebody, there's co-regulation involved, and it's intimacy. The context changed. So is it a new mixed state, or the same mixed state in a different context?
Safety plus mobility plus shutdown. All three active. You might say, "Well, Justin, that's appeasement."

Is it, though? Yes, appeasement has all those states active. But in particular, it happens with somebody else, in a life threatening context that cannot be escaped. There's a captivity element to it. All three states being active doesn't necessarily equal appeasement. Right now, I'm in all of those states. I'm immobile, but I have some mobility and some safety. I'm not in appeasement. But if somebody were here, and I was a captive, and they were threatening my life, that might turn into appeasement. Context matters. That's what I'm saying.

Now take all three states active in the context of safety, with somebody else. I'm trying to keep this G-rated: we'll call that physical intimacy. Is that now a mixed state? And what if all three states are active, but no one's there and you're alone? Again, G-rated: we might call that physical self-gratification. That might actually be more PG.

blocks.h: Mixed states, or mixed states in context?

blocks.p: So are these all mixed states now? Can we add exercise as a polyvagal mixed state? Physical intimacy? Solo physical intimacy? Or is it a mixed state in a different context?

I don't know. It kind of seems like these would all become their own mixed states. Or we could look at a context and then infer the mixed state that's happening in the individual. Instead of saying intimacy is a mixed state, we'd say the person engaging in intimate behaviors, closeness, touch, and co-regulation, may be in a stillness mixed state.
Either way, it seems like context matters. When we have a mixed state, or maybe even a primary state, the context it's in is very important.

I wish this had been covered in more depth in the new book. Appeasement, fawn, and intimacy are introduced, and mostly glossed over with some inferences about their underlying primary states or mixed states. I think there are much more interesting questions being missed: the context of the states, which I've just briefly discussed, and the potential of a behavioral adaptation versus a state or mixed state, which is the question I raised about fawn and appeasement.
